gb.name: Common Frog
gb.size: Males up to 9 cm, females up to 13 cm
gb.food: Tadpoles: algae and water fleas. Adults: slugs, snails and other invertebrates
gb.when: Spawn from January (earliest in south-west England) to April
gb.status: Common and widespread, but thought to be declining; protected from sale
gb.life: Tadpoles hatch 2 to 4 weeks after spawning, grow back legs and then front legs, and leave the water as froglets in early summer (as late as September in some ponds).
facts: A clump of spawn can hold up to 2,000 eggs, each in a jelly capsule about 1 cm across.
Colours vary a lot: yellow, pink, red, orange and even black frogs are often reported.
Older tadpoles are faintly speckled with gold, which tells them apart from the black tadpoles of the common toad.
In winter some shelter in the mud at the bottom of ponds; others hide under logs, stones or compost heaps.
learn: Amphibian and Reptile Conservation: Common frog
gb.garden: a wildlife pond with shallow, sloping edges and no fish

gb.name: Common Toad
gb.size: Males up to 8 cm, females up to 13 cm
gb.food: Adults: slugs, snails, ants, beetles, spiders and other invertebrates
gb.when: Migrates to its pond on the first warm, damp evenings of spring, a little later than common frogs
gb.status: Widespread in Britain but declining, especially in the south; a UK Priority Species; absent from Ireland
gb.life: Tadpoles hatch 2 to 4 weeks after spawning; toadlets leave the water in large numbers in early summer, usually after rain.
facts: Lays its spawn in long strings with two rows of eggs, wound round water plants.
Many walk back to the same pond their ancestors used, every spring.
Toxins in the skin of adults and tadpoles put predators off, so toad tadpoles can survive in ponds with fish.
Roads are a big danger: volunteers on 'toad patrols' help them cross on migration nights.
learn: Amphibian and Reptile Conservation: Common toad
gb.garden: a wildlife pond with shallow, sloping edges and no fish

gb.name: Smooth Newt
gb.food: On land: insects, caterpillars, worms and slugs. In water: small crustaceans, snails and tadpoles
gb.when: In ponds from February to June
gb.status: The UK's most widespread newt; protected from sale
gb.life: Larvae grow their front legs first and breathe with feathery gills; the young leave the water in late summer once the gills are gone.
facts: A female folds each egg inside the leaf of a water plant, one at a time.
Also called the common newt: the one you're most likely to find in a garden pond.
Its yellow or orange belly has neat black spots, and so does its throat (a palmate newt's throat is plain).
In the breeding season the males grow a wavy crest along the back and tail.
learn: Amphibian and Reptile Conservation: Smooth newt
gb.garden: a wildlife pond with shallow, sloping edges and no fish

gb.name: Palmate Newt
gb.size: 7 to 9 cm: the UK's smallest newt
gb.status: Widespread across most of Britain; protected from sale
gb.life: Eggs are laid singly on leaves of water plants; the larvae grow front legs first and leave the water in summer once their gills are gone.
facts: Named after the black webbing on the males' back feet in the breeding season.
Breeding males also have a thin filament at the tip of the tail.
It likes shallow pools on acid soils: heaths in the south and west, moors and bogs in the north.
Its throat is plain pink or yellow, without the spots of the smooth newt.
learn: Amphibian and Reptile Conservation: Palmate newt
gb.garden: a wildlife pond with shallow, sloping edges and no fish

gb.name: Great Crested Newt
gb.size: Up to 17 cm: the UK's largest newt
gb.status: Widespread in lowland England and Wales; strictly protected by law, eggs included; absent from Ireland
gb.life: Each female lays about 200 eggs, wrapping each one in the leaf of a water plant; the larvae are mottled with black spots and have a fine filament at the tip of the tail.
facts: The pattern of spots on its orange belly is unique to each newt, like a fingerprint.
In spring the males grow a tall, jagged crest and dance for the females, arching the back and waving the tail.
Its dark, warty skin makes it look like a mini dinosaur.
It's against the law to catch, harm or disturb one, or to damage its pond.
learn: Amphibian and Reptile Conservation: Great crested newt
The Wildlife Trusts: Great crested newt

gb.name: Natterjack Toad
gb.status: Very rare: about 60 sites in Britain; strictly protected by law
gb.life: Spawn goes into warm, shallow pools that may dry up, so the tadpoles grow fast: toadlets can develop from spawn in 6 to 8 weeks.
facts: A thin yellow stripe runs down the middle of its back.
With its short legs it runs rather than hops.
The males sing together on warm spring nights, and their rasping chorus can be heard up to a mile away.
Its spawn strings hold a single row of eggs, up to 7,500 in one clutch.
learn: Amphibian and Reptile Conservation: Natterjack toad

gb.name: Pool Frog
gb.when: Breeds in May and June, once the nights turn warm
gb.status: England's rarest amphibian; fully protected by law
gb.life: Its spawn rafts are smaller than the common frog's, with eggs brown on top and yellowish underneath.
facts: It died out in the wild in England in 1995, and was brought back to Norfolk with frogs from Sweden.
The males call loudly with a pair of balloon-like vocal sacs, one each side of the mouth.
Like its green frog relatives, it basks in the sun even on the hottest days.
Most of England's pool frogs are brown with dark blotches and a pale, often yellow, stripe down the back.
learn: Amphibian and Reptile Conservation: Northern pool frog
Amphibian and Reptile Conservation: England's rarest frog returns to Norfolk

ie.name: Common Frog
ie.size: Males up to 9 cm, females up to 13 cm
ie.food: Tadpoles: algae and water fleas. Adults: slugs, snails and other invertebrates
ie.when: Spawn from January (earliest in south-west England) to April
ie.status: Found in every county: Ireland's most widespread amphibian
ie.life: Tadpoles hatch after 3 to 4 weeks, and turn into froglets about 10 weeks later; they're ready to breed at 2 to 3 years old.
facts: A female can lay up to 4,000 eggs, and the jelly round each one keeps it up to 10°C warmer than the water.
Ireland's frogs are partly native: some survived the last ice age in an ice-free refuge in the south-west.
Males have a 'nuptial pad' on each front foot, to hold on to a female.
Older tadpoles are faintly speckled with gold.
learn: Herpetological Society of Ireland: Common Frog
Amphibian and Reptile Conservation: Common frog
ie.garden: a wildlife pond with shallow, sloping edges and no fish

ie.name: Smooth Newt
ie.food: On land: insects, caterpillars, worms and slugs. In water: small crustaceans, snails and tadpoles
ie.when: In ponds from February to June
ie.status: Ireland's only newt: its only tailed amphibian
ie.life: Larvae grow their front legs first and breathe with feathery gills; the young leave the water in late summer once the gills are gone.
facts: It's Ireland's only newt, and the only amphibian with a tail found in Ireland.
A female lays up to 300 eggs, folding each one inside a leaf of a water plant.
Its larvae grow front legs before back legs, the opposite of the common frog's tadpoles.
The young, called efts, leave the water looking like small adults, and take 2 to 3 years to grow up.
learn: Herpetological Society of Ireland: Smooth Newt
Amphibian and Reptile Conservation: Smooth newt
src: Irish Wildlife Trust: Smooth Newt Survey
ie.garden: a wildlife pond with shallow, sloping edges and no fish

ie.name: Natterjack Toad
ie.status: Ireland's rarest amphibian: naturally only on a handful of coastal sites in Kerry, with a few introduced populations
ie.life: Spawn goes into warm, shallow pools that may dry up, so the tadpoles grow fast: toadlets can develop from spawn in 6 to 8 weeks.
facts: Ireland's only toad, and its most endangered native amphibian.
A yellow line runs the length of its back, which the common frog doesn't have.
Its short legs mean it can't hop like a frog.
Unlike the common frog, it staggers its breeding: some toads breed early in the season, others later.
learn: Herpetological Society of Ireland: Natterjack Toad
Amphibian and Reptile Conservation: Natterjack toad

us.name: American Bullfrog
us.size: 9 to 20 cm (3.5 to 8 in): the largest frog in North America
us.food: Insects, crayfish, snails, small fish, other amphibians, and even small birds and mammals
us.when: Breeds from late spring through summer
us.status: Native to the eastern and central United States; invasive where it has been introduced in the West
us.life: Tadpoles are large and may take 1 to 3 years to become frogs: often two winters in the water.
facts: The male's deep call sounds like 'jug-o-rum'.
A female can lay up to 20,000 eggs in a floating, jelly-like mass.
Males have yellow throats, females white.
Grabbed by a predator, it lets out a loud, piercing scream.
learn: National Park Service: American Bullfrogs Fast Facts
Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Bullfrog

us.name: Green Frog
us.food: Tadpoles: algae and detritus. Adults: insects, spiders, worms, crayfish, slugs and small frogs
us.when: Breeds from March to September
us.status: Common; not of immediate conservation concern
us.life: Females lay 1,000 to 7,000 eggs in floating sheets; the tadpoles turn into frogs in about 3 months.
facts: Its call is a twangy 'plunk', like a loose banjo string.
Often bronze rather than green, so it's also called the bronze frog.
Ridges running from the eyes down the back tell it apart from a young bullfrog.
Males defend territories with calls, posturing and wrestling.
learn: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Green / Bronze Frog

us.name: Northern Leopard Frog
us.when: Males start calling in late April
us.status: Once the most widespread frog in North America, now declining in many places
us.life: A female can lay more than 6,000 eggs; the young frogs leave the water by early August to feed on land.
facts: Named for its round, light-edged spots, like a leopard's.
In summer it may wander 1 to 2 miles from water into wet meadows and grassland.
Its call is a long, deep snore that ends in chuckles.
Minnesota has spotless leopard frogs too: the 'Burnsi' colour form.

us.name: Wood Frog
us.when: Breeds in late winter or early spring, sometimes before the ice has melted
us.status: Widespread and secure
us.life: Lays its eggs in pools that dry up by midsummer, so the tadpoles have to hurry: 40 to 90 days to become frogs.
facts: It survives being frozen: its liver makes so much sugar that its cells aren't damaged, while its heart stops and it stops breathing.
It lives farther north than any other amphibian in the Western Hemisphere, above the Arctic Circle.
Its call sounds like a duck's quack.
A dark mask runs from its snout through each eye.
learn: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Wood Frog
National Park Service: Tiny Masters of Arctic Survival

us.name: Spring Peeper
us.when: Breeds in late winter and early spring
us.status: Abundant and widespread
us.life: Breeds in shallow, fish-free wetlands: marshes, seasonal ponds and ditches.
facts: Named for the X on its back, though it's more often an imperfect X.
Its high-pitched 'peeep', rising at the end, is one of the first sounds of spring.
Much of its body can survive freezing in winter.
It copes with some towns and suburbs, if there are trees and fish-free ponds.
learn: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Spring Peeper
us.garden: a wildlife pond with shallow, sloping edges and no fish

us.name: Gray Treefrog
us.food: Tadpoles: algae and detritus. Adults: insects, spiders, snails and slugs
us.when: Calls from late April to early August
us.status: Widespread, with a large population
us.life: Eggs hatch in 3 to 7 days, and the tadpoles turn into frogs in 45 to 65 days.
facts: It changes colour, green, gray or brown, with temperature and activity.
It spends the winter in trees and survives freezing by making glycerol.
Sticky pads on its toes help it climb.
Bright yellow or orange under its legs may startle predators.
learn: Smithsonian's National Zoo: Gray tree frog

us.name: Pacific Treefrog
us.when: Calls year-round except in the driest and coldest weather
us.status: Secure: the most widespread frog in Washington
us.life: Lays small, loose packets of 9 to 70 eggs on plants in still water; the tadpoles grow to about 5 cm before they change.
facts: Also called the Pacific chorus frog; its call is a two-part 'rib-it'.
Its choruses can be heard from a long way off.
It has toe pads on its fingers and toes for climbing.
Usually green or brown, but gray, red and copper ones turn up too.
learn: Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife: Pacific treefrog
us.garden: a wildlife pond with shallow, sloping edges and no fish

us.name: American Toad
us.food: Tadpoles: algae and detritus. Adults: ants, beetles, moths and earthworms
us.when: Breeds from March to July in most of its range
us.status: Least Concern: widespread and tolerant of disturbed land
us.life: Its eggs hatch in 3 to 12 days, and the tadpoles become toadlets in 1 to 2 months.
facts: Lays 2,000 to 20,000 eggs in long double strings.
Its tadpoles often swim in dense schools for safety.
The male's call is a long, musical trill that can last 30 seconds.
Its skin and even its eggs contain toxins.
learn: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): American Toad
us.garden: a shallow, fish-free pond and some leaf litter

us.name: Fowler's Toad
us.when: Breeds in spring and early summer, after heavy rain
us.status: Common across most of its range
us.life: Lays long strings of eggs, sometimes more than 25,000; they hatch within days, and the tadpoles change in about two months.
facts: Its call is a short, nasal bleat, like a sheep.
It has at least three warts in each dark spot on its back (an American toad has one or two).
It's mostly out on warm, humid summer nights.
It hybridizes with the American toad where the two live together.
learn: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Fowler's Toad

us.name: Western Toad
us.food: Tadpoles: algae and detritus. Adults: mostly insects, and worms
us.when: Breeds from mid-April at low elevations, later higher up
us.status: Locally common, with declines in some places
us.life: A female lays about 12,000 eggs in long strings; the tadpoles school with their brothers and sisters and change in about two months.
facts: Newly changed toadlets leave their pond together for one to two weeks.
A single car can kill thousands of toadlets crossing a road.
Its parotoid glands, behind the eyes, make a poison that puts predators off.
Grabbed, it gives a 'release call'.
learn: Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife: Western toad

us.name: Pickerel Frog
us.when: Breeds from late March to early May
us.status: Stable across most of its range
us.life: Lays balls of 700 to 3,000 eggs on underwater plants; the tadpoles take about 87 to 95 days to become frogs.
facts: Two rows of square dark spots run down its back (a leopard frog's are round).
Its skin secretions are toxic to predators and can irritate human skin.
Bright yellow or orange under its hind legs may startle a predator.
Its call is a low, nasal snore.
learn: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Pickerel Frog

us.name: Eastern Newt
us.food: Invertebrates at every stage, including mosquito larvae
us.when: Breeds in late winter and early spring
us.status: Widespread, but threatened locally by habitat loss and disease
us.life: Larvae live in water for 2 to 5 months, then turn into land-living efts, which become aquatic adults after 2 to 3 years.
facts: Its young spend years on land as a bright orange red eft, whose colour warns that its skin is toxic.
A female lays 200 to 400 eggs one at a time on water plants.
Adults turn yellowish-green but keep the red, black-ringed spots.
It can live 12 to 15 years.
learn: New York State DEC: Eastern (Red-Spotted) Newt
Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Red-spotted Newt

us.name: Rough-skinned Newt
us.when: Courtship mostly in March and April at low elevations; after the snow melts higher up
us.status: Common, with no widespread declines
us.life: Females lay their eggs one at a time and hide them in water plants; newts are the last salamanders to breed and to hatch each year.
facts: Its skin is full of a strong poison, tetrodotoxin, that few predators survive (the common garter snake is the exception).
Threatened, it bends its head back towards its tail to show its bright orange belly.
It's the only salamander in Washington that hides its eggs in plants.
Wash your hands after touching one, and keep it away from small children.
learn: Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife: Rough-skinned newt

us.name: Spotted Salamander
us.when: Walks to its breeding pool on rainy nights in winter and early spring
us.status: Common across most of its range
us.life: Lays clumps of up to 200 eggs in pools without fish; they hatch in 4 to 8 weeks, and the larvae change in 2 to 4 months.
facts: Algae living in its egg masses make oxygen for the growing embryos.
It spends most of its life underground and is rarely seen outside the breeding season.
It can live about 20 years.
It needs temporary pools: fish would eat its eggs and larvae.
learn: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Spotted Salamander

us.name: Jefferson Salamander
us.size: 12 to 20 cm, half of it tail
us.when: Moves to its pond on the first warm, rainy nights of spring (late March or early April)
us.status: Of conservation concern in parts of its range
us.life: Lays clumps of eggs on underwater plants in woodland ponds; the larvae lose their gills by midsummer and leave for the forest.
facts: It can live up to 30 years.
It spends the winter below the frost line in rodent burrows or cracks in rock.
It may have blue flecks on its sides and legs.
It needs clean ponds that don't dry up in summer.

us.name: Northern Two-lined Salamander
us.size: About 8 cm, half of it tail
us.when: Breeds in autumn or spring; lays its eggs in spring
us.status: Least Concern; no sign of widespread declines
us.life: Lays 20 to 50 eggs under submerged rocks, and the female often stays with them until they hatch, 1 to 2 months later; the larvae can take up to three years to grow up.
facts: A lungless salamander, which dries out quickly, so it stays close to its stream.
A yellowish stripe down its back is edged by two black lines.
Its short, stocky legs suit fast-flowing water.
In summer it may wander a few hundred metres from its stream to hunt, and many are killed on roads.

us.name: Southern Leopard Frog
us.when: Breeds mainly in winter and spring, sometimes again in autumn
us.status: Common and widespread in the Southeast
us.life: Breeds in almost any shallow freshwater, especially wetlands without fish.
facts: Heavy winter rain can set off a burst of breeding.
Often seen crossing roads in large numbers on rainy nights.
Its call is a guttural, chuckling croak, like a low laugh.
It can live far from water and even tolerates slightly salty water.
learn: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Southern Leopard Frog

us.name: Green Treefrog
us.when: Breeds from March to October
us.status: Least Concern: common, with stable populations
us.life: Males call from water plants and branches up to 5 m above weedy ponds and swamps.
facts: On warm, rainy nights it hunts the insects drawn to porch lights.
Bright green, often with a pale stripe along each side.
Its call is a loud, nasal 'reeenk, reeenk'.
It has spread into new areas with potted plants and pine straw.
learn: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Green Treefrog

us.name: Cope's Gray Treefrog
us.when: Breeds from March to August, peaking in early summer
us.status: Widespread and abundant
us.life: Breeds in fish-free wetlands such as woodland pools.
facts: It looks exactly like the gray treefrog: the two are told apart by their calls, Cope's being faster and buzzier.
It has two sets of chromosomes; the gray treefrog has four.
It changes from mottled gray to light green.
Wash your hands after holding one: its skin can irritate eyes and cuts.
learn: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Cope's Gray Treefrog

us.name: Northern Cricket Frog
us.when: Breeds in spring and summer
us.status: Common in the Southeast, declining in parts of the Midwest
us.life: Lives along the edges of shallow, weedy ponds, lakes and slow streams.
facts: Its call sounds like marbles clicking together.
A small, warty frog without toe pads: it hardly ever climbs.
Males fight over territories in the breeding season.
A jagged stripe on its thigh tells it from the southern cricket frog.
learn: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Northern Cricket Frog

us.name: Eastern Spadefoot
us.when: Comes up to breed after heavy rain, at almost any time of year
us.status: Locally common in the Southeast; of concern farther north
us.life: Lays up to 2,500 eggs in temporary pools and puddles; the tadpoles can become toadlets in as little as 28 days.
facts: It spends most of the year underground, digging with a hard, dark spade on each hind foot.
Its call is a low, nasal 'waaah', made while floating on the water.
Some people say it smells like peanut butter.
Handling one can make some people sneeze and wheeze.
learn: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Eastern Spadefoot Toad

us.name: Oak Toad
us.size: About 4.4 cm (1.75 in): the smallest toad in North America
us.when: Breeds in shallow pools after heavy rain
us.status: Generally common in pine forests, but vulnerable to their loss
us.life: Breeds in shallow, fish-free pools formed by heavy rain.
facts: Unlike most toads, it's active by day.
Its call is a high-pitched chirp from a vocal sac that balloons out.
A light stripe runs down the middle of its back.
It lives in sandy pine forests of the southeastern Coastal Plain.
learn: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Oak Toad

us.name: California Red-legged Frog
us.size: Up to 13.8 cm (5.4 in): the largest native frog in the western United States
us.food: Tadpoles: algae. Adults: insects and other invertebrates; big ones eat treefrogs and mice
us.when: Breeds from November to May, mostly during or after heavy rain
us.status: Threatened (US Endangered Species Act, 1996); gone from 70% of its former range
us.life: Each egg mass holds 300 to 4,000 eggs, and fewer than 1% survive the tadpole stage.
facts: Mark Twain's 'Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County' is thought to be this frog.
Named for the red of its belly and hind legs.
It has been brought back to the Santa Monica Mountains, where it now breeds on its own again.
Non-native bullfrogs, crayfish and fish are among its biggest threats.
learn: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service: California Red-legged Frog
National Park Service: California Red-Legged Frogs

us.name: California Newt
us.size: 7 to 9 cm (2.75 to 3.5 in) snout to vent
us.food: Larvae: small water invertebrates. Adults: worms, snails, slugs, insects, and amphibian eggs
us.when: Lays eggs from November to July
us.status: A California Species of Special Concern
us.life: Lays balls of 7 to 47 eggs that hatch in 14 to 52 days; the larvae spend several months in the water and leave at the end of summer.
facts: Its skin makes tetrodotoxin, the same poison as a pufferfish's.
It's found only in California, along the coast from Mendocino to San Diego County.
Pale yellow to orange underneath, with rough, grainy skin.
The young leave their pond and aren't thought to return to water until they breed.

us.name: Eastern Tiger Salamander
us.when: Breeds in open, grassy ponds
us.status: Widespread, but less common in the Southeast
us.life: The larvae grow astonishingly fast, reaching 13 to 15 cm in a couple of months before they change.
facts: One of the largest land salamanders.
Usually black with yellow spots, blotches or bars.
It's more often found as eggs or larvae than as an adult.
In the Southeast it seems never to keep its gills as an adult.
learn: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Tiger Salamander

us.name: Marbled Salamander
us.when: Breeds in autumn (September and October), unlike most mole salamanders
us.status: Common, but threatened by habitat loss
us.life: Lays 30 to 100 eggs in a dry hollow; the female stays with them until rain fills it, and the larvae take 2 to 9 months to change.
facts: If no rain comes, its eggs can wait through the winter until spring.
Like many salamanders, it has poison glands in its tail.
It spends most of its life underground.
It needs fish-free, temporary pools.
learn: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Marbled Salamander

us.name: Northern Dusky Salamander
us.when: Lays its eggs under streamside debris
us.status: Common
us.life: Its eggs are laid on land beside a stream, and the larvae finish growing in the water.
facts: It hides under logs and rocks by day and moves along stream banks at night.
It usually has 6 to 8 pairs of golden spots on its back.
A lungless salamander, living in and near cool streams.
Males court females by rubbing them with a gland on the chin.
learn: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Northern / Spotted Dusky Salamander

ca.name: Boreal Chorus Frog
ca.when: Breeds very early in spring, often before the ice has melted
ca.status: Least Concern; not believed to be in significant decline
ca.life: Lays 150 to 800 eggs in small clusters; they hatch within a few weeks, and the tadpoles change in about two months.
facts: Its call sounds like a fingernail run along the teeth of a comb.
It can survive being frozen.
One of the first frogs out in spring, calling day and night.
Until 1989 it was thought to be the same species as the western chorus frog.

ca.name: Blue-spotted Salamander
ca.food: Insects, spiders, worms and other invertebrates
ca.when: Breeds in early spring in woodland ponds and swamps
ca.status: Not at risk; a Specially Protected Amphibian in Ontario
ca.life: Lays 200 to 500 eggs in small clusters on water plants; they hatch in 3 to 4 weeks and the larvae change by midsummer.
facts: Black or gray-brown with bluish-white spots.
Some hybrid females have three, four or five sets of chromosomes.
Some of those hybrids have young that are clones of their mother.
It spends the winter underground in the forest.

ca.name: Eastern Newt
ca.food: Invertebrates at every stage, including mosquito larvae
ca.when: Breeds in late winter and early spring
ca.status: Widespread, but threatened locally by habitat loss and disease
ca.life: Larvae live in water for 2 to 5 months, then turn into land-living efts, which become aquatic adults after 2 to 3 years.
facts: Its young spend years on land as a bright orange red eft, whose colour warns that its skin is toxic.
A female lays 200 to 400 eggs one at a time on water plants.
Adults turn yellowish-green but keep the red, black-ringed spots.
It can live 12 to 15 years.
learn: New York State DEC: Eastern (Red-Spotted) Newt
Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Red-spotted Newt

ca.name: American Bullfrog
ca.size: 9 to 20 cm (3.5 to 8 in): the largest frog in North America
ca.food: Insects, crayfish, snails, small fish, other amphibians, and even small birds and mammals
ca.when: Breeds from late spring through summer
ca.status: Native in eastern Canada; introduced (and a problem) in British Columbia
ca.life: Tadpoles are large and may take 1 to 3 years to become frogs: often two winters in the water.
facts: The male's deep call sounds like 'jug-o-rum'.
A female can lay up to 20,000 eggs in a floating, jelly-like mass.
Males have yellow throats, females white.
Grabbed by a predator, it lets out a loud, piercing scream.
learn: National Park Service: American Bullfrogs Fast Facts
Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Bullfrog

ca.name: Gray Treefrog
ca.food: Tadpoles: algae and detritus. Adults: insects, spiders, snails and slugs
ca.when: Calls from late April to early August
ca.status: Widespread, with a large population
ca.life: Eggs hatch in 3 to 7 days, and the tadpoles turn into frogs in 45 to 65 days.
facts: It changes colour, green, gray or brown, with temperature and activity.
It spends the winter in trees and survives freezing by making glycerol.
Sticky pads on its toes help it climb.
Bright yellow or orange under its legs may startle predators.
learn: Smithsonian's National Zoo: Gray tree frog

ca.name: Mink Frog
ca.when: Breeds from late spring to midsummer
ca.status: Least Concern; thought to be stable
ca.life: Lays a ball of 500 to 2,000 eggs on water plants; the tadpoles take one to two years to become frogs.
facts: It gives off a musky smell, like a mink.
Its call is a quick series of croaks, like a hammer tapping on wood; a big chorus sounds like popcorn popping.
It lives in big, cold, weedy ponds, lakes and bogs, and spends the winter underwater.
It looks very like a green frog, but its belly is yellowish and its legs unbanded.

ca.name: Pickerel Frog
ca.when: Breeds from late March to early May
ca.status: Stable across most of its range
ca.life: Lays balls of 700 to 3,000 eggs on underwater plants; the tadpoles take about 87 to 95 days to become frogs.
facts: Two rows of square dark spots run down its back (a leopard frog's are round).
Its skin secretions are toxic to predators and can irritate human skin.
Bright yellow or orange under its hind legs may startle a predator.
Its call is a low, nasal snore.
learn: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Pickerel Frog

ca.name: Pacific Treefrog
ca.when: Calls year-round except in the driest and coldest weather
ca.status: Yellow-listed (secure) in British Columbia
ca.life: Lays small, loose packets of 9 to 70 eggs on plants in still water; the tadpoles grow to about 5 cm before they change.
facts: Also called the Pacific chorus frog; its call is a two-part 'rib-it'.
Its choruses can be heard from a long way off.
It has toe pads on its fingers and toes for climbing.
Usually green or brown, but gray, red and copper ones turn up too.
learn: Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife: Pacific treefrog
Province of British Columbia: Frogs & Toads
ca.garden: a wildlife pond with shallow, sloping edges and no fish

ca.name: Western Chorus Frog
ca.when: Calls from mid-March, mostly in April, sometimes while there's still ice
ca.status: The Great Lakes–St. Lawrence population is Threatened (Species at Risk Act)
ca.life: Lays 400 to 1,500 eggs in loose masses; they hatch within a few weeks, and the tadpoles change by early or midsummer.
facts: Its call sounds like running a fingernail along the teeth of a comb.
It can survive being frozen.
It has declined by 37% in Quebec since the 1950s, mainly through habitat loss.
Three dark stripes run down its back.

ca.name: Canadian Toad
ca.when: Breeds in May and June
ca.status: 'May Be At Risk' in Alberta
ca.life: Lays up to 20,000 eggs in shallow water; they hatch in about a week, and the tadpoles become toads in 6 weeks.
facts: Hundreds may spend the winter together in mounds, in burrows below the frost line.
A hard bump (a 'boss') between its eyes tells it from the American toad.
It's more at home in water than most toads, around prairie wetlands.
Its trill is like an American toad's, but lower and shorter.
learn: Government of Alberta: Amphibian species at risk

ca.name: Western Toad
ca.food: Tadpoles: algae and detritus. Adults: mostly insects, and worms
ca.when: Breeds from mid-April at low elevations, later higher up
ca.status: Yellow-listed in British Columbia; declines in some places
ca.life: A female lays about 12,000 eggs in long strings; the tadpoles school with their brothers and sisters and change in about two months.
facts: Newly changed toadlets leave their pond together for one to two weeks.
A single car can kill thousands of toadlets crossing a road.
Its parotoid glands, behind the eyes, make a poison that puts predators off.
Grabbed, it gives a 'release call'.
learn: Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife: Western toad

ca.name: Rough-skinned Newt
ca.when: Courtship mostly in March and April at low elevations; after the snow melts higher up
ca.status: Common, with no widespread declines
ca.life: Females lay their eggs one at a time and hide them in water plants; newts are the last salamanders to breed and to hatch each year.
facts: Its skin is full of a strong poison, tetrodotoxin, that few predators survive (the common garter snake is the exception).
Threatened, it bends its head back towards its tail to show its bright orange belly.
It's the only salamander in Washington that hides its eggs in plants.
Wash your hands after touching one, and keep it away from small children.
learn: Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife: Rough-skinned newt

ca.name: Spotted Salamander
ca.when: Walks to its breeding pool on rainy nights in winter and early spring
ca.status: Common across most of its range
ca.life: Lays clumps of up to 200 eggs in pools without fish; they hatch in 4 to 8 weeks, and the larvae change in 2 to 4 months.
facts: Algae living in its egg masses make oxygen for the growing embryos.
It spends most of its life underground and is rarely seen outside the breeding season.
It can live about 20 years.
It needs temporary pools: fish would eat its eggs and larvae.
learn: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Spotted Salamander

ca.name: Long-toed Salamander
ca.when: May be the earliest-breeding amphibian in British Columbia, crossing snow to its pond
ca.status: Secure (Yellow-listed) in British Columbia
ca.life: Lays up to 400 eggs, singly or in small clusters; they hatch in 2 to 3 weeks, and at high elevations the larvae may spend the winter in the pond.
facts: A yellow-green or orange-green stripe with ragged edges runs down its back.
It lays its eggs before the ice has fully melted.
It lives 6 to 10 years.
When it changes, it absorbs its gills and tail fins and starts breathing with lungs.

ca.name: Western Tiger Salamander
ca.when: Comes up from underground on warm spring rains
ca.status: Southern Mountain population Endangered (Species at Risk Act)
ca.life: Lays 100 to 5,000 eggs in clusters; they hatch in 2 to 3 weeks, and most larvae change in late summer.
facts: Some larvae never leave the water: they grow up keeping their gills.
When food is short, some larvae grow big mouths and teeth and eat other larvae.
Larvae seem to avoid eating their own brothers and sisters, perhaps by smell.
It can live more than 25 years.
learn: B.C. Reptiles & Amphibians: Western Tiger Salamander

ca.name: Northern Two-lined Salamander
ca.size: About 8 cm, half of it tail
ca.when: Breeds in autumn or spring; lays its eggs in spring
ca.status: Least Concern; no sign of widespread declines
ca.life: Lays 20 to 50 eggs under submerged rocks, and the female often stays with them until they hatch, 1 to 2 months later; the larvae can take up to three years to grow up.
facts: A lungless salamander, which dries out quickly, so it stays close to its stream.
A yellowish stripe down its back is edged by two black lines.
Its short, stocky legs suit fast-flowing water.
In summer it may wander a few hundred metres from its stream to hunt, and many are killed on roads.

ca.name: Fowler's Toad
ca.when: Breeds in spring and early summer, after heavy rain
ca.status: Endangered: in Canada only on three peninsulas on the north shore of Lake Erie
ca.life: Lays long strings of eggs, sometimes more than 25,000; they hatch within days, and the tadpoles change in about two months.
facts: Its call is a short, nasal bleat, like a sheep.
It has at least three warts in each dark spot on its back (an American toad has one or two).
It's mostly out on warm, humid summer nights.
It hybridizes with the American toad where the two live together.
learn: Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (University of Georgia): Fowler's Toad
Government of Canada: Recovery Strategy for the Fowler's Toad

ca.name: Jefferson Salamander
ca.size: 12 to 20 cm, half of it tail
ca.when: Moves to its pond on the first warm, rainy nights of spring (late March or early April)
ca.status: Endangered in Canada
ca.life: Lays clumps of eggs on underwater plants in woodland ponds; the larvae lose their gills by midsummer and leave for the forest.
facts: It can live up to 30 years.
It spends the winter below the frost line in rodent burrows or cracks in rock.
It may have blue flecks on its sides and legs.
It needs clean ponds that don't dry up in summer.

ca.name: Great Basin Spadefoot
ca.when: Breeds from April to July
ca.status: Threatened (Species at Risk Act)
ca.life: Breeds in temporary and permanent ponds; its tadpoles are gray and round with gold flecks.
facts: It digs into the ground with a sharp-edged dark spade on each hind foot.
It shelters in burrows by day and through dry spells.
In Canada it lives only in the dry valleys of south-central British Columbia.
Its eyes have vertical pupils.
learn: Government of Canada: Recovery Strategy for the Great Basin Spadefoot

ca.name: Coastal Tailed Frog
ca.when: Lives in cold, fast mountain streams
ca.status: Special Concern in Canada; Blue-listed in British Columbia
ca.life: Its tadpoles cling to rocks in fast water with a round, sucker-like mouth, and can take up to 4 years to change.
facts: The male's 'tail' is really an organ for mating.
It has no voice.
It can live up to 20 years, one of the longest-lived frogs.
Its closest living relatives are in New Zealand.
learn: Province of British Columbia: Frogs & Toads
